h1:
Hat Yai Shopping Plan
Kim Yong–Santi Sukh–Malls–ASEAN Night Bazaar
intro: Hat Yai has been the shopping town of southern Thailand for decades. Malaysian families drive across the border just to shop here, because everything sits within walking distance — from the old souvenir market of Kim Yong to the clothes-and-cosmetics market of Santi Sukh, big air-conditioned malls, and night markets you can stroll all evening. This plan spreads it over 2 days, going zone by zone so you're not running back and forth.

blocks.html: The charm of shopping in Hat Yai is that everything is packed into the city centre. The Niphat Uthit 1–2–3 area all connects on foot, with plenty of hotels nearby — you can walk it, or hop on a motorbike taxi or tuk-tuk just as easily. This plan splits the day into market and mall shopping during daylight, then saves the night market for the evening — because each spot keeps different hours, so getting the order right means you won't waste a trip.

blocks.text: Before you set off — what's open when

blocks.html: What a lot of people get wrong is that the opening and closing hours aren't the same everywhere. Plan the order badly and you'll show up to a locked gate. Here's the quick rundown first.

items: Kim Yong Market — open daily, roughly 06:00–18:00. Before 10am it's fresh produce and fruit; later in the morning it shifts fully to souvenirs → walk it in the morning.
Santi Sukh Market — open roughly 09:00–20:00, right next to Kim Yong so you can walk straight over → continue here during the day after Kim Yong.
Malls (Central / Lee Gardens / Odean) — open roughly 10:00/11:00–21:00/22:00 → escape the afternoon heat and rest your legs inside.
ASEAN Night Bazaar — open Tue–Sun, roughly 16:00–22:00, closed Monday → save it for the evening of day one.

blocks.title: The smoothest order
blocks.html: Morning: walk Kim Yong once the souvenirs are fully out → midday: cross over to Santi Sukh → afternoon when the sun is harsh: duck into a mall to rest your legs in the cool air → evening: finish at the ASEAN Night Bazaar, eating and shopping as you stroll.

blocks.text: Day 1 — half a day of souvenirs, half in the malls, finish at the night market

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Kim Yong → Santi Sukh → malls → ASEAN Night Bazaar

items.activity: Breakfast near Kim Yong, then start walking the market
items.note: There are plenty of dim sum and congee shops in front of the market — eat up first and the walk is easier on the stomach.

items.activity: Walk Kim Yong Market and tick off all your souvenirs
items.note: The footpath out front is lined with stalls of nuts, cashews, dried plums, dried fruit and imported chocolate. Inside it's dried goods, processed seafood, and tea and coffee.

items.activity: Cross over to Santi Sukh Market in the Niphat Uthit area
items.note: This zone is strong on clothes, bags, shoes, perfume, cosmetics and small electronics — plus goods from Malaysia and Indonesia to choose from.

items.activity: Break for lunch in the area
items.note: Around Niphat Uthit you'll find chicken rice, dim sum and southern Thai restaurants — eat somewhere close by so you don't waste time walking.

items.activity: Head into Central Festival Hat Yai to escape the afternoon heat
items.note: The biggest mall in the lower south, with the full range of brands, cold air-con and easy walking. There's a souvenir zone with nicely packed gifts if you want things ready to carry onto the plane.

items.activity: Stop by Lee Gardens Plaza or Odean for more shopping
items.note: Lee Gardens is right in the city centre, with a night market starting to set up around it. Odean leans younger, with cute, affordable clothes.

items.activity: Take a ride to the ASEAN Night Bazaar on Chotwittayakul Road
items.note: It's near the Hat Yai bus terminal — a few minutes from the centre by motorbike taxi or taxi. Open Tue–Sun, closed Monday.

items.activity: Walk the ASEAN Night Bazaar — shop for fashion and grab street food
items.note: Clothes, bags, shoes, watches and accessories at easy prices, plus a food court on the 2nd floor where you can sit and refuel.

items.activity: Back to the hotel, pack your souvenirs
items.note: Pack the dry goods now; leave anything that needs refrigeration for the day you head home.

blocks.title: If you come on a Monday
blocks.html: The ASEAN Night Bazaar is closed Mondays, so swap in a night market around Lee Gardens or the Greenway Night Market instead — same walk-eat-shop vibe.

blocks.text: Day 2 — pick up what you missed + morning market before heading home

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Morning at Kim Yong → grab souvenirs → mall before leaving

items.activity: Head back to Kim Yong Market in the morning for fresh produce and fruit
items.note: Early morning is the fresh-produce window, with seasonal southern fruit. Pick what you want to eat fresh today; you can keep buying dried souvenirs where you left off yesterday.

items.activity: Make the rounds for the specific souvenirs you had in mind
items.note: You scoped out the prices on day one, so buying for real today feels more confident. Compare 2–3 shops before buying in bulk.

items.activity: Stop by a mall for nicely packed gifts + anything that needs air-con
items.note: Boxed snacks and brand-name souvenirs — buying them in the mall means they're ready to carry onto the plane, no wrapping needed.

items.activity: Last meal, double-check your souvenirs before the trip home
items.note: Run through the souvenir checklist one more time, in case you forgot something for the boss or a friend — go grab it in time before leaving town.

blocks.text: The Hat Yai souvenirs people take home most

blocks.html: If you don't know where to start, these are the souvenirs you see people hauling out of Kim Yong the most, ordered from easiest to buy and most likely to please. Prices are rough ranges and depend on the shop and season — you can haggle if you buy a lot.

items.name: Cashews / roasted nuts
items.blurb: One of Kim Yong's top souvenirs — salted, honey-roasted, and plenty of shops where you can taste before you buy. Easy to carry, keeps well, and a hit with almost every age group.
items.meta: Stalls in front of Kim Yong Market

items.name: Pistachios / almonds / macadamias
items.blurb: Graded imported nuts sold by the kilo, great for splitting into small bags to give to several people. Cheaper here than in a regular mall.

items.name: Dried squid / salted fish / processed seafood
items.blurb: Dried goods from the southern sea — dried squid, salted fish, good-quality shrimp paste. Things southerners are proud of, perfect for people who love to cook.

items.name: Dried plums, dried fruit, peaches, raisins
items.blurb: Sweet-and-sour snacks to nibble on the road, with plenty of styles to grab. Easy to buy and not pricey.

items.name: Imported chocolate & snacks from Malaysia/Indonesia
items.blurb: Imported snacks that are hard to find in other cities — chocolate, biscuits and treats from across the border. Kids love them.

items.name: Tea & coffee (teh tarik, old-style coffee)
items.blurb: Teh tarik mix and southern-style coffee you can brew at home for that Hat Yai cafe taste. An easy gift for any coffee lover.

items.name: Southern chilli pastes & curry pastes
items.blurb: Southern-style curry and chilli pastes that pack real heat — a winning gift for anyone who cooks. Sold both pre-packed and by the scoop.

items.name: Clothes, bags, shoes (Santi Sukh / ASEAN Night)
items.blurb: Not food, but people haul plenty home — fashion clothing, bags and shoes at easy prices. You can browse all day at Santi Sukh and the ASEAN Night Bazaar.

blocks.title: Haggling like a Hat Yai local
blocks.html: At Kim Yong and Santi Sukh, if you're buying several things or going big, just tell the vendor straight that you'd like a better price — you'll usually get a freebie or a discount. Walk 2–3 shops to compare before you commit, and always check the expiry dates on dry goods.

blocks.text: Which zone for what — the short version

items.name: Kim Yong
items.blurb: Edible souvenirs — nuts, snacks, processed seafood, tea and coffee. Open morning to evening.

items.name: Santi Sukh
items.blurb: Clothes, bags, shoes, perfume, cosmetics and small electronics.

items.name: Malls (Central/Lee Gardens/Odean)
items.blurb: Brands, air-con, nicely packed gifts ready for the plane, and shade from the afternoon sun.

items.name: ASEAN Night Bazaar
items.blurb: Affordable fashion + a 2nd-floor food court — eat and shop as you stroll in the evening.

blocks.text: Good to know before you shop

items: Carry cash — most market stalls take cash and PromptPay, but some small shops still don't take cards.
Bring an empty bag — pack a big bag or canvas tote; people buy Hat Yai souvenirs several bags at a time.
Buy chilled items on the way out — salted fish and fresh seafood are best bought on your last day before catching the bus or plane, so they don't spoil en route.
Avoid the midday sun — open-air markets get very hot from 12:00–15:00; ducking into a mall to rest is far more comfortable then.
Check for Mondays — the ASEAN Night Bazaar is closed Mondays, so plan your days carefully.

faq.q: What's the difference between Kim Yong and Santi Sukh markets?
faq.a: Kim Yong focuses on edible souvenirs — nuts, snacks, dried fruit and processed seafood — while Santi Sukh focuses on clothes, bags, shoes, perfume and cosmetics. The two sit right next to each other in the Niphat Uthit area, so you can walk straight between them in a single trip.

faq.q: What time of day is best for shopping in Hat Yai?
faq.a: Morning to late morning for Kim Yong's souvenir market when everything is out, midday cross over to Santi Sukh, afternoon when the sun is harsh duck into a mall to rest your legs, then save the ASEAN Night Bazaar for the evening since night markets open from around 16:00 onwards.

faq.q: Is the ASEAN Night Bazaar open every day?
faq.a: No — it's open Tue–Sun, roughly 16:00–22:00, and closed Monday. If you land on a Monday, head to a night market around Lee Gardens or Greenway instead.

faq.q: Which Hat Yai souvenirs are easy to buy and please everyone?
faq.a: Cashews and roasted nuts are the top pick — easy to carry and they keep well. Next come dried fruit, dried plums, imported snacks, tea and coffee, and processed seafood for anyone who loves to cook.

faq.q: Can you haggle at Hat Yai markets?
faq.a: Yes, especially when you buy several things or go big. Just ask the vendor for a better price and you'll usually get a freebie or a discount. It's worth comparing 2–3 shops before committing, and always check the expiry dates on dry goods.
